Verify with `command -v herdr` and `herdr --version`. - **Skill.** Link the `herdr` skill into the shared skill root and every agent's skills folder, the same way other skills are linked. The skill lives at `skills/herdr/SKILL.md` in the herdr repo. It is what tells an agent how to drive Herdr; without it, the review recipe has no instructions to follow. - **Server.** Start the Herdr server and confirm it is running with `herdr status`. The review commands need a live server. The server starts when Herdr launches; if `herdr status` reports it not running, start it per the herdr docs. - **Agent integration.** For an agent to be recognized and controlled inside a Herdr pane, install its integration with `herdr integration install ` (for example `hermes`, `codex`, `claude`). This gives session-resume after a server restart and reliable lifecycle state. ## Rex Rex (Superlogical, beta) is the second host for the independent review. Inside a Rex pane (`REX_SESSION` set) and outside Herdr, `herdr-review.sh` hands off to `rex-review.sh` (`before-push.md`, "In Rex"). - **App and CLI.** The macOS app is open to beta testers (`https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/installation`). The app ships the `rex` CLI and puts it on the path of its own panes. Verify with `rex whoami --json` from a Rex pane. - **Skill.** `rex skill setup` installs a `rex` skill stub that runs `rex __internal skill`, the guide for the installed version. - **What it cannot tell.** Rex shows the status a program reports with OSC 7501 (`https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status`). On 2026-10-24 Claude Code reported one; Kimi Code 2.3.1, the Cursor agent CLI 2026.10.22 and Codex CLI 0.164.0 did not. So `rex-review.sh` reads the reviewer's state from the pane's process and the bottom of its screen, and a reported status, when one appears, comes first. ## Herdr app (hc) The Herdr app is the third host for the independent review. It runs on herdr-core, whose CLI is `hc`, and is a separate program from Herdr TUI: the two share no terminals (herdr.dev FAQ, "How is it different from Herdr TUI?", 2026-10-29). In an hc terminal (`HC_TERMINAL_ID` set) outside Herdr TUI and Rex, `herdr-review.sh` hands off to `hc-review.sh` (`before-push.md`, "In the Herdr app"). - **App and CLI.** Install from `https://herdr.dev/download/`. Verify with `command -v hc` and `hc server status`. - **Guides.** `hc --skill` prints the current manual for driving agents with `hc`; `~/.config/herdr-app/AGENTS.md` covers the window itself (layouts, keys, mods). - **What it tells.** `hc get ` gives a status only for a program that reports one with OSC 7501. On 2026-10-29 Codex CLI 0.166.0 reported one and the Cursor agent CLI 2026.10.22 did not; Kimi Code was not checked. `hc-review.sh` reads a reviewer that reports none from its screen. # Guardrails Read this when a project lacks a shared tool, a check script, CI or a review standards file, or when you are about to write a one-off script to count or classify something. ## A project with nothing yet A repository with no `AGENTS.md`, no check script and no CI is not a reason to work without them. It is the case this skill exists for, and building them is the first work on such a repository. One concern per pull request, in this order: Start at the first step you do not find, not at step 1. A repository that already has `AGENTS.md` resumes at step 2, and only the steps still missing are the work. **The order is not finished until every step exists**: a session that lands one of them has not discharged it, and the next session picks up at the first step still missing. 1. **`AGENTS.md`.** The project's working rules and pointers. Keep it short: it points at other files rather than restating them. Start from the session-start list in `SKILL.md`, keep what applies, drop what does not, and add what this project needs. Every project's `AGENTS.md` carries two standing rules so all agents working in the repo behave the same, regardless of which agent they are: - **Writing.** Before writing anything a person will read, load the `clear-writing` skill and follow it — every reply, status update, email, doc, README, commit and PR description, post, and any text the user asks to edit. It applies to subagents too. - **Working on a repository.** Before changing anything, load the `way-of-working` skill and follow it — how decisions get recorded, the pull request every change goes through, the checks before each push, the independent review before a PR opens, watching an open PR until it merges, and the retro that improves the standard. 2. **`scripts/check.sh`, CI and the pre-push hook.** One script running every mechanical gate, called by both CI and the hook, so a local run and a CI run cannot differ. The sections below have the detail and the conditions for installing the hook. **The hook's install line goes into the `AGENTS.md` you wrote at step 1** — the project's own file, so a fresh clone of that project can wire the hook. It never goes into this skill: the install line names one project's path, and every other repository loads this skill. 3. **The shared tool** for the figures the project's documents quote, with its tests. 4. **A review standards file.** Near-empty at first. It grows from findings a reviewer actually made, each with the incident that taught it. An incident is a claim about the past, so read the commit or run the command that shows it before writing it. A first draft of one such file named the wrong evidence three times — a figures tool faulted for a record its count comparison did not read, a guard faulted for a blind spot its own status line already covered, a repair faulted for losing blob ids it had never stored — and each was rewritten only after the history was read. The commits stay in that project's own file; the rule here is what to do before writing one. 5. **Decision records.** A folder with an index, and agreement with the owner on how a skipped question is read (`references/deciding.md`). **The first pull request is the exception.** Rule 3 and `before-push.md` require the check script to pass before every push, and on a bare repository there is not one yet — an agent that treats this as absolute cannot push at all. Until step 2 lands, the check before a push is the project's own build and test command; if the project has none, say so in the pull request body rather than implying one ran. Nothing else about the flow changes: one concern, a pull request, the owner merges. The check script starts with the gates the project already has. It gains the shared tool's consistency checks when step 3 lands, not before — the tool does not exist yet, and a check script that names a missing tool fails on its own first run. Say what you are about to do and why before the first of these lands. An owner who did not ask for a check script is owed the reason, and may have one already. The work you were asked to do is not lost by this: it waits behind the guardrails, and lands on a repository where every later change is checked. ## Shared, deterministic tools Every agent that writes its own counting script counts differently, and each difference becomes a wrong figure in a document. Build one tool in the repo instead, and make every agent use it. - **What it answers:** the figures documents quote, one item's status, the items in one work item, a repo-wide search that also matches text split across lines, and consistency checks such as decision records against their index. - **How it computes:** run the project's existing scripts as they are (in a temporary copy if they write files) rather than reimplementing their logic. Define each population once, in code, from the source file's structure. - **What it prints:** the files it read and the commit, so a PR body can quote the line; `--json` for agents. - **How it is trusted:** tests that pin today's figures, tests that break the input on purpose (reformatting, citations, wrapped lists) and expect the same answer, and a test that the tool never writes to the repo. Before writing any script to count or classify, check whether the shared tool already answers the question. If it does not, extend the tool, not a private script. ## One check script, run everywhere - One script runs every mechanical check: the project's gates, all tests, the shared tool's consistency checks, and a test that published figures in documents match the tool. - It fails if the checks change the working tree. Comparing content hashes is not enough by itself: a guard built that way passed every ordinary run while missing four changes — an untracked file rewritten (names were recorded, not contents), a file named `-` (a bare `-` operand is read as standard input even after `--`), a dropped executable bit, and an index change. Snapshot four things and fail on any difference, each pinned to what it has to observe: - **Contents.** Open each non-ignored path, tracked or untracked, and hash the bytes read. Do not hand the path to a hasher that may read standard input: `sha256sum -- -` hashes empty input, so an untracked file named `-` can be rewritten with the snapshot unchanged. - **Filesystem entry, not the file behind it.** An untracked script that loses its execute bit changes neither its contents nor git's status. A symlink retargeted to a different path holding the same bytes changes neither, because opening it follows the link. Snapshot the entry type, the permission bits, and for a symlink the link text itself — read the link, not through it, and keep its **exact bytes**. A shell's `$(readlink -- link)` drops a trailing newline, so a retarget to a target name ending in one hashes the same before and after; `os.readlink` and `stat -c '%N'` keep it and see the change. - **Index blobs.** `git status` records a change *category*, not a blob id: a staged blob can be replaced while the porcelain letter is already `MM`. Snapshot the blob id and mode of every index entry (`git ls-files -s`). - **git's own view of status**, which covers renames and staging the four above do not name directly. A read that fails **aborts the comparison**. Skipping the path drops it from both snapshots, so they match, and a check that rewrote a file the guard could not read still passes. A language where reads raise gives that for free; in a shell the status must be taken from the read itself, because a pipeline's status is its last command's, not the failing one's. - CI runs it on every PR. A pre-push hook runs it locally. **Give the hook a way to be installed** — a `scripts/bootstrap.sh` that sets `core.hooksPath` and installs anything the checks need, or, if the project prefers fewer files, the one-line `git config` command written into the project's `AGENTS.md`. Either way say where it is, and put it in the session-start steps of the project's `AGENTS.md` (step 2 of the order above): a hook nobody installs is a hook that never runs, and a fresh clone is exactly where that happens. - Set up the hook only in the simple case, where all of these hold: `git config core.hooksPath` prints nothing; `ls "$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks)"` shows only `*.sample` files; no tool installs hooks (Git LFS, pre-commit); and `git worktree list` shows one worktree. In any other case, change no hook configuration: report what you found and ask the owner how to wire the check in, because an existing or shared hook setup can serve other worktrees or repositories. - In the simple case: add `scripts/hooks/pre-push` that runs the check script, track it as executable (`git update-index --chmod=+x scripts/hooks/pre-push`; `git ls-files -s` shows `100755`), and set `git config core.hooksPath scripts/hooks`. Git silently skips a missing or non-executable hook, so a successful push proves nothing. Have the hook skip a push whose every ref is a delete: git passes one line per ref on standard input, a delete's local object name is all zeros, and a delete sends no commits to check. On one project, deleting eleven merged branches took 90 minutes of checks. A run with no lines, as `git hook run pre-push` gives, still runs the checks. - **Tests that build their own git repository must drop inherited `GIT_*` variables.** Git runs a hook with `GIT_DIR` set, and absolute inside a worktree, so a test's `git -C ` follows it to the repository being pushed: its `init`, `config` and `commit` land there. Remove every `GIT_*` variable before the test's first git call, and test that a decoy `GIT_DIR` is left untouched. - Prove the hook runs: `git hook run pre-push` (Git 2.36 or later) must print the check script's output and exit 0. Then make one check fail on purpose and confirm `git hook run pre-push` exits non-zero; restore it. - Pin CI actions to tags that exist (check with `gh api repos///git/ref/tags/`). ## Mechanical rules in code, judgement in a review file Classify each rule. A rule a script can check (a figure, a status match, a required section, a file pattern) goes in the check script. A rule that needs judgement (a claim matches its record, a change landed, the right population was counted) goes in a short review standards file the reviewer reads, each rule with the incident that taught it. The review file references the instruction file's requirements; it does not restate them. ## Done when The project has the shared tool with tests, the check script running in CI and the hook, and a review standards file holding only judgement rules. # Changing Read this before opening a pull request. ## The flow 1. Branch from the current main. 2. Make one concern's change. A follow-up fix found while working goes in its own PR unless it is the same concern. 3. **Refine the code before review.** Run the `ce-simplify-code` skill on the change. It launches three parallel reviewers (code-reuse, code-quality, efficiency), applies worthwhile findings while preserving behavior, verifies with typecheck/lint/tests, and summarizes. This is the pass that makes the diff reviewable — do it before the checks below, so the independent review reads the code you intend to ship, not a first draft. Skip it only when the change is documentation, generated or vendored files, or mechanical churn with no substantive code (the skill's own preflight decides). 4. Run the checks in `before-push.md`. 5. Open the PR. Its body carries what "What the body says" below lists. That section is the one place that says what a body holds. 6. Watch the PR until it merges. See "Watching a pull request" below. 7. After merge, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/after-merge.sh ` and move to the next item. **When a PR must merge one way, make it the only way the repository allows.** A file that pins one of the PR's own commits breaks under a squash or rebase merge, which give that commit a new SHA. A warning in the PR body is not enough: a PR that carried one at the top was squash-merged anyway, and a follow-up PR had to re-pin. Ask the owner to untick "Allow squash merging" and "Allow rebase merging" in the repository settings, so the default merge button is the right one. ## Who reviews Each pull request gets two reviews: the independent review before each push (`before-push.md`), and the PR review, which gives the merge verdict. The scripts are in `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/`. Whether the Cursor bot is available decides which tool does which: | Cursor bot | Independent review: the first available, in this order | PR review | |---|---|---| | Available | 1. Kimi on K3.1 Pro at high effort: `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`
2. Pi: `pi-review.sh --role independent`
3. Codex on gpt-6-luna: `herdr-review.sh` | The Cursor bot | | Not available | 1. Kimi on K3.1 Pro at high effort: `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`
2. Codex on gpt-6-luna: `herdr-review.sh`
3. The Cursor agent CLI: `herdr-review.sh --kind cursor` | Pi: `pi-review.sh --role pr` | Each order leaves out the tool that gives the PR review, so rule 5 below holds whichever reviewer runs. A reviewer is not available when it cannot start here, when its run fails with an error (Pi through Ollama returns 429 at its weekly usage limit), or when it gives no report within its hour and has stopped. `pi-review.sh` stops Pi at the hour itself. When `herdr-review.sh` ends without a report, run its `Next:` command first, because the review may still be running; the reviewer counts as not available only when that command also ends without a report and `herdr agent get ` shows the reviewer idle or done, not working (in Rex, first read `rex block call -s -b program_status` and keep waiting while it says working or blocked; then confirm with `rex block call -s -b process` whether the reviewer's program still runs; only then do two looks a minute apart with `rex capture -s -b ` that show the same screen, with the reviewer's empty input line and no busy marker, count as idle; in the Herdr app, `hc get ` shows the terminal finished, or its status idle or done, and for a reviewer that reports no status, two looks a minute apart with `hc read ` show the same screen with its empty input line). While it is still working, keep waiting for it. Then try the next one in the order. When every reviewer in the order is not available, push nothing: tell the owner, and wait for a reviewer that differs from the PR reviewer. `herdr-review.sh` runs in a Herdr TUI pane, inside Rex, where it hands off to `rex-review.sh`, or in the Herdr app, where it hands off to `hc-review.sh`. Outside all three, Kimi and the Cursor agent CLI are not available, and Codex runs through the Codex plugin, as `before-push.md` says. Say in the PR body which reviewer ran, and why each one before it in the order did not. 1. **Before the pull request opens, pick the row from what the bot did on the repository's most recent pull request**, the newest one by creation, whether it is open, merged or closed. If the bot posted a review of the head commit, or merged the pull request itself, within 20 minutes of that pull request's last push, the mark in rule 2, use the "Available" row, even when that review counted only as a comment there. If it did not, use the "Not available" row. A merged pull request still shows every time this needs: - the head commit: `gh pr view --json headRefOid,mergedAt,mergedBy`, which also shows a merge by the bot; - the last push: `gh api repos///commits//check-suites`, each suite's `created_at`. A commit's own date is when it was written, which can be long before its push; - the check's start: `gh pr checks --json name,startedAt`; - each review's commit and time: `gh api repos///pulls//reviews`. A review of an earlier commit does not count. Judge the bot's behaviour, not the row that pull request used: a pull request on the "Not available" row reads the bot's answers as comments, so copying its row would keep every later pull request on that row after the bot came back. For a repository's first pull request, use the "Available" row. On the "Not available" row, Pi is the PR reviewer from the first push: start it on every push without waiting for the bot, and read any answer from the bot as a comment. 2. **After each push, give the bot 20 minutes.** A bot that has not answered at 9 minutes may still be reviewing (the owner, 2026-10-30: "the fact that Cursor did not get back in 9 mins does nt mean cursor bot stops reviewing it"). `merge-on-verdict.sh --timeout 1200 --bot-check "Cursor Automation"` waits for its verdict (the bot's check is named "Cursor Automation" on this owner's repositories). The bot is not available when it has posted no verdict 20 minutes after the push (exit 5), or sooner when its check has finished without one, skipped or "encountered an error" (exit 7), since then it is no longer reviewing. 3. **When the bot is not available, start Pi as the PR reviewer yourself, on top of what the bot already did:** `pi-review.sh --role pr --pr --head `, with `--since ` after the first round. Read everything the bot and its companions (Bugbot) posted on the pull request first, fix or answer each finding, and give the reviewer that list with what became of each item, so it checks those and goes on from there instead of starting over. Nothing starts it for you. Its MERGE or HOLD comment is the answer you wait for on that push. If the script exits 1, run it once more; if it fails again, log it and leave the pull request open. 4. **A switch lasts for the rest of the pull request. Stop the bot's run on that head before its stand-in starts**, so two reviewers do not work on one push or race their verdicts. When `merge-on-verdict.sh --bot-check` exits 7, or exits 5 saying "with no verdict from" the bot (an exit 5 that says it was waiting for the check "with the bot's MERGE in hand" is not a missing verdict: wait for the check, and switch nothing), and before `pi-review.sh --role pr` (or the stand-in the project names) starts: 1. Run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/stop-cursor-review.sh ` from the repository, or with `--repo `. It finds the bot's agent through the bot's check run on that head, cancels the agent's latest run through Cursor's Cloud Agents API, and adds the label `review-takeover` to the pull request, creating the label if the repository lacks it. It reads the API key from `CURSOR_API_KEY` or from `~/.config/cursor/api.env`; never commit the key. It leaves Bugbot and other Cursor agents alone. Exit 3 means something could not be checked or done, such as no key, no bot check run or a cancel the API refused, and says what: start the stand-in anyway, since the owner's recipe makes the switch even when the stop fails, and the bot may then still answer; read that answer as a comment. Exit 4 means the pull request is no longer at that head: start no stand-in for it, and wait for the bot on the new head. 2. Where the bot is a Cursor Automation, its owner adds a rule once per repository in the Cursor dashboard: skip pull requests labelled `review-takeover`. Without that rule, the next push starts the bot again. Tell the owner if the rule is missing. 3. Do not convert the pull request to a draft as the stop. A draft does not cancel a run already in progress. From then on the stand-in gives the verdict on every push, and the independent review follows the "Not available" row's order. A later answer from the bot is read as a comment, not as the verdict. 5. **The two reviews of the merged commit come from different tools.** Its independent review and its merge verdict must not both come from Pi, or both from Cursor. When the row changes after an independent review ran, and the tool that ran it now gives the PR review, run the first available reviewer in the new row's order on the head commit at once, and fix or answer its findings. Check again before you merge. The project or the owner can name other reviewers; the same rules then apply to the ones they name. When a reviewer in the order is not available, tell the owner which one and why, in the PR body or the session's report. `pi-review.sh` runs Pi in a fresh clone under `/tmp`, never in the working tree, because a reviewer that checks out a commit changes the files under your feet. As the independent reviewer it can review a commit that is not pushed yet, named by a short or full hash; it writes a report whose first line is READY or FIX, and posts nothing. A `--since` that names no commit, or that does not reach the clone, stops the run before Pi starts. As the PR reviewer it posts one comment whose first line is MERGE or HOLD, whose second line is `Reviewed commit: `, and whose last line is a mark unique to the run; the script fails unless a comment with that mark, that first line and that commit appears on the PR. A comment that names a commit other than the head is a verdict on that older commit. `--verify ""` names what to check, as for `herdr-review.sh`. Inside Herdr, Pi runs in its own tab, `pi--`, so the owner can watch; the tab closes only when every check passed. As the PR reviewer it refuses a `--head` that is not the pull request's head, and fails if the head moved while Pi reviewed. Pi gets an hour, then the script stops it and exits 1. It stops the whole process group, because `ollama launch` runs Pi as a child and does not pass the signal on; inside Herdr, that is the tab's foreground group. A passed run removes its clone. As the independent reviewer it keeps its report and prints the path as `Report:` on standard error, so output cut short can be read again. A failed run keeps the clone and its log to read. It needs Ollama and Pi installed (`ollama launch pi`). `scripts/test_pi_review.py` covers each case. ## What the body says The body carries these: - **What changed, and why.** The shape of the change in a line or two, then the problem it answers. - **What the checks found, including the independent review.** Which findings it raised, and what became of each. - **Any judgement call the reviewer should weigh.** Which findings you fixed and which you answered, with the reasoning the reviewer needs to weigh the answer. This one is prose, and prose stays. - **The shared tool's commit line for every figure.** Quoted, so the reader can re-run it. - **Whether the code was refined.** "Simplify: ran on " and what it changed, or why it was skipped, so a skipped refinement pass ("The flow", step 3) shows. Three things make that readable. - **The smallest view that makes the point.** A diff sketch, a call tree, a file tree or a short table says more than paragraphs, because the reader is checking a shape rather than reading an argument. Pick the one that answers the question they have, and leave the other views out. - **Evidence, before and after.** Not "verified" — the output. The failing run and the passing run, or the command and what it printed. Evidence the reader can re-run beats a claim they must trust, and it is the difference between a reviewer checking your work and taking your word. - **Merge danger.** A one-way door or a two-way one? A change that is cheap to revert is lower risk, and the owner deciding whether to merge needs to know which this is. Add the blast radius in a word or two: what it touches, and who will notice. This shape is adapted from the `pr` skill in `mattpocock-skills` (itself from Humanlayer's `show-me`). Its template is not adopted wholesale: this section already owns what a PR body contains, and a second copy of one rule is what rule 6 forbids. ## Watching a pull request Watch every pull request you open, and every one already open when you start, until it merges or the owner closes it. A pull request nobody watches sits on a review finding for hours. - **While the Cursor bot is the PR reviewer, wait up to 20 minutes after each push for its verdict**, as "Who reviews" says, with `merge-on-verdict.sh --timeout 1200 --bot-check "Cursor Automation"` (exit 5: 20 minutes passed with no verdict; exit 7: the bot's check finished with none; after a MERGE the deadline becomes the later of start + `--timeout` and start + one hour, and an exit 5 then says it was waiting for the check, not for the bot), because `watch-pr.sh` does not wake on a check that only starts. If it is not available (exit 7, or exit 5 with no verdict from the bot; an exit 5 with its MERGE in hand is only a slow check), stop its run with `stop-cursor-review.sh` ("Who reviews", rule 4). On its exit 0 or 3 start Pi as the PR reviewer yourself; on its exit 4 the pull request has a new head, so start nothing and wait for the bot on that head. The 20 minutes is the wait for a verdict; the stop is what keeps the bot from reviewing on after its stand-in starts, and when the stop fails (exit 3) any later answer from the bot is a comment. - **Run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/watch-pr.sh `** from the repository as a background job the harness reports back on. It polls every 30 seconds and exits on the first new event: a merge or close, a new review, conversation comment or inline review comment, or a check that finishes, including a rerun that finishes with the same result. A check that only starts or reruns wakes nothing. It exits at once if the pull request has already merged. When it exits, read what changed, act, and start it again unless the pull request is merged or closed. Report only changes; silence is the normal case. - **Where the project lets you merge on the PR reviewer's verdict, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/merge-on-verdict.sh `** as a background job, from the pull request's repository or with `--repo `. It waits for the bot's MERGE or HOLD review on that head (older commits never count; leading HTML comments are stripped), then for the required check (`--check`, default `checks`), and merges with `--match-head-commit` only on MERGE plus a passed check. It never bypasses branch rules, with one exception the owner must authorize: `--admin-if-only-review` lets it merge with admin privileges when GitHub refuses the merge because a required approving review is missing (for example, an approval agent that asks for a human on medium-risk changes) and nothing else is open: every check on the head passed, the head is not behind its base where the base's rules require an up-to-date branch (the script reads the rules and compares, since GitHub reports BLOCKED, not BEHIND, while a review is also missing), and no current review thread is unresolved. Ask the owner once whether they want that; if they do, record their words in a decision record, pass the flag on every merge, and the script says so in a comment on each pull request it merges this way. It never merges past a HOLD, a failed or pending check, a required update from the base, an open thread or a new head. When an admin merge must wait, it says why once (for example, an unresolved review thread or a check that has not passed), so a wait that will never end shows. Where the project requires a section in every PR body, pass `--require-section `: the script merges only when the body, as GitHub renders it, has a heading with exactly that text, ignoring the case of ASCII letters only ("État" does not match "état"). GitHub's renderer decides what is a heading, so a line in a code block or a comment never counts. Its exit code says what stopped it: 0 merged at the given head, by it or by someone else; 1 closed without a merge, or gh failed ten times in a row; 2 a HOLD; 3 a failed check; 4 a new head, or a pull request merged at another head (the wrong repository's pull request of that number); 5 timed out (with `--bot-check`: no verdict within `--timeout`, or, after a MERGE, the required check not finished by the later of start + `--timeout` and start + one hour; the message says which); 6 the body lacks the required section; 7 with `--bot-check`, the bot's check finished with no verdict, so start its stand-in; 64 a usage error. A loop written for the occasion is how a merge on a failed check gets through. - **Bound review output.** Use `gh api --jq` to select the reviewed commit, creation time, state, and relevant body text. Omit decorative HTML footers. Keep unresolved findings from earlier commits available until fixed or answered. Retrieve source text needed to judge a finding even when it is from an older round. - **After each push, leave the pull request alone until its reviewer answers**, with a hold or a merge. Make no other push, force-push, rebase or edit to its description in the meantime: a change that lands while the reviewer reads makes its verdict name a commit that is no longer the head, and the round is wasted. Work on something else while y ... command output truncated for persistence ... u write it, not after. 3. **External facts cite a primary source.** Release notes, a changelog, a specification or a filing, with version and date. An open issue, a roadmap or a search snippet is a lead, not a source. A version claim names the first release with full support, not a preview. For anything hosted on GitHub, read it with `gh api` (releases, tags, file contents). Read the primary source itself, not a page about it: on one PR a README's "Version 1 Beta" heading stood in for an ontology file whose maturity annotation said Released. Quote the governing file or filing, and quote the passage whole: the sentence as the source prints it, so its qualifiers come with it. 4. **A change reaches every place it applies.** Search the whole repo for every status, rule, term or figure you change, including text split across lines. When you change a rule, walk every section that depends on it: later pipeline steps, checklists, examples, companion documents, other repos that copy it. When a change adds a member to a set of values (an enum value, a status, a category) or replaces an instruction, also search for the bare old number, the set's other members, and the old instruction's own words, such as the ticket a step used to wait for. A search for the phrases you expect finds only those phrases. If the project's fact tool has a sweep command, run it first: it lists where the wording the branch replaced or deleted still stands. It cannot see the same claim in other words, a one-word change or an addition, so the searches above stay required. Search record header rows and text split across lines too: on one PR a record's header kept an old count that its body had corrected, and on another a count split across two lines escaped a one-line search. Report what you searched in the PR body, under the heading the project requires (for example "Sweep"). 5. **Every command the change tells a person to run has been run.** For a runbook, README steps or a guide, run each command, or a harmless version of it (a dry run, a read-only query, a check against a throwaway copy), in the shell the reader uses (zsh on macOS, where `status` is a read-only variable), and check its exit status on the failure path as well as the success path. Say in the PR body which commands ran, and what each printed. *Why:* on one PR, a stores runbook took four review rounds, and most findings were commands nobody had run: a loop that passed silently on failure, a variable zsh refuses, a readiness check that exited 0 when the database never answered, and table names pasted into SQL unquoted. 6. **An independent review runs on the diff, and every finding is fixed or answered.** Use a different model from the one that wrote the change. The table under "Who reviews" in `changing.md` says which reviewers to try, in order, and when one counts as not available. For Kimi, run `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`, described below. When it names Pi, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/pi-review.sh --role independent --head --verify ""`, with `--since ` for a later round, as a background job, and read its report; that section describes the script. For Codex, run `herdr-review.sh` with no `--kind`. When it names the Cursor agent CLI, use `herdr-review.sh --kind cursor`. The table decides the tool; the host only decides where it runs. `herdr-review.sh` runs when the working agent is inside a Herdr TUI pane (`test -n "${HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID:-}"`, which is what the script checks); inside a Rex pane, where it hands off to `rex-review.sh` ("In Rex" below); or in a terminal of the Herdr app, where it hands off to `hc-review.sh` ("In the Herdr app" below). Outside all three, Kimi and the Cursor agent CLI are not available, and Codex runs through the Codex plugin, described below. **Commit the change first, and leave the working tree clean.** A branch review reads committed commits only, so an uncommitted fix is not reviewed at all — an agent that reviews, then edits, then pushes has reviewed the wrong thing. Note the commit you reviewed; if HEAD moves before the push, review again, within the round limit under "Re-review after fixing" below. **With Herdr** (the working agent is inside a Herdr pane), spawn a reviewer agent in its own pane — a different kind/model from the writer — and have it run the `ce-code-review` skill, which does a structured multi-agent review (risk-based reviewer selection, parallel reviewers, a cross-model adversarial pass, a validator, and a rendered report). **Reuse the review tab for this repo and reviewer rather than opening a new one for every review.** It is named `review---` (the repo's directory name, then the reviewer's kind and a hash of its kind and model) so it is findable: ```sh # From the repository under review, as a background job the harness reports back on # (Claude Code: run_in_background), never with `&`: a review outlasts a foreground call. ~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/herdr-review.sh --branch --verify "" ``` `scripts/herdr-review.sh` opens or reuses that reviewer's `review---` tab in this agent's own workspace and starts a reviewer only in an empty pane. With no `--kind`, the script starts Codex on gpt-6-luna at medium reasoning, the owner's choice, set in the script. `--kind` and `--model` pick another reviewer. Every reviewer, the default too, has its own tab, because a reused pane keeps the model it started with: a new default model opens a new tab, never the old default's. A `review-` tab with no kind or hash is from before this rule, when the default reviewer had no hash; close it once (`herdr tab close `). A hashed tab from before keeps its meaning, because its name already came from its kind and model. Each kind starts with its own flags: - **Codex:** `-a never` (no approval prompts) and the `workspace-write` sandbox with network. The sandbox may also write to `~/.npm`, `~/.claude`, `~/.cache` and `~/.config`, which the review skill's cross-model pass needs. - **Cursor** (`--kind cursor`, default model cursor-grok-4.6-medium): `--sandbox enabled --force --trust`, which is sandboxed, with no approval prompts and the workspace trusted. - **Kimi** (`--kind kimi`, default model kimi-code/k3.1-pro, which runs at high effort, its default): `-y`. Kimi has no sandbox, and `-y` still asks before risky actions. A fresh Kimi can ask a one-time setup question, such as migrating `kimi-cli` data, that blocks the first prompt. Leave that choice to the owner, answer it with `herdr agent send-keys`, and run the script again. The script then tells the reviewer to apply the repository's review standards, waits until the reviewer is idle with its report written, and prints the report. Before it prompts, it prints `Report file: ` on standard error, so the report stays findable when the output is cut short. Whatever the prompt returns (completed, stalled, blocked or timed out), the script runs one recovery, so a review finishes unattended: - **A Cursor prompt left pasted but unsent** (the input line reads `→ [Pasted text #1 +1 lines]`) gets an Enter. The script reads the visible screen on every poll until the reviewer starts work, whatever the status says, and sends Enter on each poll where the input line still shows the marker, up to three Enters. It acts only for `--kind cursor` and only on the input line, so the marker quoted elsewhere on screen, such as in a diff, sends nothing. On 2026-10-23 herdr read the pane as idle, and the text appeared after the first look. - **It waits** until the reviewer has worked and gone idle, within 60 minutes of the start. - **A reviewer idle without the report** is asked once to write it at the path. - **However the wait ends**, a non-empty file the reviewer wrote at the path is printed once its size holds steady, and is never overwritten. The script gives a missing or empty file a minute to fill. - **Still missing or empty:** it copies a `report.md` that `ce-code-review` saved under `/tmp` or `$TMPDIR` (`compound-engineering-/ce-code-review//`), says so on standard error, and prints it. The script header states which one counts: one written after the script started, whose `metadata.json` names this branch and the commit the script started on, and only when exactly one qualifies. Zero or several end in exit 1. **An earlier review can hold the reviewer's name.** Herdr refuses a name another live agent holds and names the holder's tab, directory and status. When the holder is in this work tree and idle or done, the script closes its tab (`herdr tab close`), prints `closed (status )` on standard error, and starts once more. The retry always runs: closing the holder restarts the five tries a busy pane gets. When closing another tab fails, the script prints herdr's error and still retries once. When closing the reused review tab fails, the script prints herdr's error, creates no tab, and stops, with `Next:` closing that tab and then running the script again. The holder can be the reused review tab itself, whose pane reads as having no reviewer while herdr still holds the name; the script then closes that tab, creates a fresh one, prints `Review tab: (created)`, and starts there. When it is still working or blocked, the script stops without closing it: `Reviewer did not start: another review is running in ; wait for it or close it.`, then a `Next:` line that waits for that review and runs the script again. A holder in another directory is left alone, and the start fails with herdr's error. Exit 0 means the report, and only the report, is on standard output. Exit 1 means no report, and every exit 1 ends with two lines: the reason, then `Next: `. After the prompt, the output ends with `Prompt result: ` (only if the prompt did not complete), the pane's recent text, then `No report at : .` and the `Next:` line. Before the prompt, a reviewer that did not start prints herdr's error and the pane, then `Reviewer did not start: .` and the `Next:` line. Any other early failure (`HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID` unset, a herdr error, no review tab or pane, an unwritable report folder) prints its error on standard error, then `No review: failed; the error is above.` and the `Next:` line. The same two lines end a run that fails or is killed (TERM, INT or HUP, even during the prompt's own wait) once the prompt is on its way. `Next:` then waits for that review and prints its report if the prompt was delivered (it returned, or the reviewer was seen working), and runs the script again if not. Exit 2 means bad arguments. `scripts/test_herdr_review.py` covers each of those cases. **Wait for the job's exit status and output before you push or open a pull request.** Launching it returns neither. A non-zero status stops the push. **When it ends without a report**, read the reason, act on it, and run the `Next:` command: `herdr agent wait ... && cat ''` when the review may still be running; `cat ''` when the reviewer's file was still growing; the script again with the same arguments when the reviewer never started or finished without a report; an answer to the reviewer's question (`herdr agent send-keys `) followed by the wait when it blocked after working, or by the script again when it was blocked before the prompt arrived; and, when several skill reports match, a `cp` of the one you pick after reading them. The review tab shares the working tree, so the reviewer sees the branch you have checked out. For later rounds, run it again with the new commit and say which findings you fixed or answered (see "Re-review after fixing" below). `ce-code-review` is report-only, so apply its findings yourself. Setup notes: - **The writer can drive the reviewer only with an allow rule.** Claude Code's auto mode blocks starting or prompting an agent that never asks for approval. The owner adds `Bash(herdr agent:*)` once per machine through `/permissions`. - **`-a never` stops command-approval prompts.** Execution failures go back to the reviewer instead, so the owner is never asked to approve its commands. - **The cross-model pass needs those writable folders.** Under plain `workspace-write`, `ce-code-review`'s Claude cross-check failed with `npm error code EPERM` on `~/.npm`, so the review fell back to an adversarial pass from the same model family. The folders clear that error: on 2026-10-13, `npx -y acpx@0.19.4 --version` failed with EPERM in the plain sandbox and printed `0.19.4` with the folders. That check does not prove the whole cross-model pass runs. If a report says it did not run, say so in the PR body. - **The script runs from a private copy of itself.** Bash reads a script while it runs, and the skill's `scripts/` folder is a working tree, so before this a commit, checkout or edit of `herdr-review.sh` during a review broke the running review; on 2026-10-24 one did. A test rewrites the script mid-run and expects the report. - **A review tab opened before this setting keeps its old sandbox.** The script says so when it reuses a running reviewer. Close that tab once (`herdr tab close `), and the next run starts a reviewer with the current flags. **Close the review tab when the PR merges.** The script prints `Review tab: (created|reused)` on standard error. If this agent's run created it, send the reviewer a "PR merged" message, then `herdr tab close `. Do not close a tab you did not create. **In Rex** (the working agent is inside a Rex pane, `REX_SESSION` set, and not inside Herdr), run the same command. `herdr-review.sh` hands its arguments to `rex-review.sh`; `--host rex` or `--host herdr` overrides the choice. It starts the same reviewers, with the same flags and the same prompt; `test_rex_review.py` runs both scripts and fails when what they launch or send differs. What changes: - **Where the reviewer opens.** The first reviewer opens as a split to the right of this agent's pane, without taking focus. When that window already holds two panes, the reviewer opens in a new tab instead (the owner's layout, 2026-10-24). The pane is labelled `review----`. It is reused only while this kind's program runs in it, started in this work tree. A labelled pane whose program has exited, or which shows a shell, is closed and replaced; if the close fails, the script stops. A labelled pane running anything else, or a reviewer in another directory, is left alone and the script stops. The script prints `Review pane: (created|reused)`. - **How the script knows what the reviewer is doing.** Rex shows only a status a program reports (OSC 7501), and the reviewer CLIs report none, so the script reads the pane's process and the bottom of its screen, in this order: the program exited; rex could not answer (unreadable); Kimi's usage-limit error (limit: the run stops with "Reviewer not available: it reports its usage limit." and a Next line naming `pi-review.sh --role independent`); a reported status of blocked or working; Kimi's question about resuming an idle session; Kimi's folder-trust dialog naming this work tree on its own path line, the one between its question and its choices; a question on screen; a busy marker (`ctrl+c to stop`, `esc to interrupt`, `Running agents`, `Agent Running`; on a reused pane the script keeps waiting while one shows, up to 45 minutes, instead of spending its usual budget of looks, and then takes that earlier review's report when it matches the branch and HEAD); the reviewer's own input line still holding the prompt (unsent); a screen that changed since the last look; the reviewer's own empty input line (idle); anything else that stays put (unknown, treated as a question). Each reviewer's input line is its own: Kimi's boxed `│ >` with its `context:` line, read whole from the box's top border to its bottom border, because a long prompt wraps over many lines inside it; a prompt longer than the box scrolls inside it (its top border reads "↑ 13 more"), and then the box counts as holding the prompt when its visible text ends with the prompt's last sentence, "Then reply with that path.", Cursor's `→ Plan, search, build anything` or `→ Add a follow-up`, and Codex's `›` line. Codex's idle text was not seen live, because its hook review stood in the way, so any `›` line not holding the prompt counts as ready. - **Nothing is typed unless the screen calls for it.** The prompt goes in only when the reviewer's own empty input line shows, in a new pane or a reused one, with no other question or choice list on the bottom lines: Kimi's data-migration question above its input line is a question. Every Enter comes right after a fresh look of the pane, and is held if that look shows anything other than the state the Enter answers; a look that catches the screen still redrawing is taken again, up to five times a second apart. Kimi's question about resuming a session left idle ("Compact and continue", "Start a new session", "Continue as-is") gets "Start a new session"; when it shows after the prompt was sent, the prompt is sent again. An unsent prompt gets Enter, up to three times; Kimi left one unsent on 2026-10-24. Three unanswered Enters end the run. Kimi's "Trust this folder?" gets "Trust and continue" once, and only when the dialog's own path line, between its question and its choices, names this work tree, because the owner said on 2026-10-24: "it is okay to always trust the folder and continue". Any other question or unknown screen before the prompt, such as Codex's hook review, which approves code rather than a folder, stops the script with `Reviewer did not start: it is waiting on a question or an unknown screen.` Answer it, or leave it to the owner, and run the script again. - **When the report counts.** The report counts once two looks see it at the same size while the reviewer is neither working nor blocked. Asking for the report, or deciding it never comes, waits for six idle looks in a row, 30 seconds, because a reviewer can work quietly. A question, a trust dialog and an unknown screen all count toward the same two minutes of waiting on a question, and a wait that runs out while one shows ends as waiting on a question. A run that ends blocked, exited, unsent or unreadable never prints the file at the report path, which may be partial, and never falls back to the review skill's report. - **The exits are the same:** 0 with the report alone on standard output, 1 with the reason and a `Next:` line, 2 for bad arguments, including an option without a value or a host other than `rex`. `Next:` reads the pane with `rex capture` where Herdr's would wait with `herdr agent wait`. **Close the review pane when the PR merges:** `rex block close -s `, only for a pane your run created. **In the Herdr app** (the working agent runs in an hc terminal, `HC_TERMINAL_ID` set, and neither `HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID` nor `REX_SESSION` is set), run the same command. `herdr-review.sh` hands its arguments to `hc-review.sh`; `--host hc` overrides the choice. The Herdr app runs on herdr-core, whose CLI is `hc`; it is a separate program from Herdr TUI and shares none of its terminals. Same reviewers, flags and prompt, plus Codex's `--no-daemon`, which hc needs; `test_hc_review.py` fails when what the two scripts launch or send differs. What changes: - **Where the reviewer runs.** Each run starts a fresh child terminal of this agent's (`hc run --bg --no-notify`), named `rev--`; it shows under this agent in the app and ends with it. A live terminal holding that name in this work tree that is idle or done is ended and removed first; one working, blocked or reporting no status stops the script ("another review is running"); one in another directory is left alone. The script prints `Review terminal:
()`. - **How the prompt goes in.** Codex and the Cursor agent get it as their launch task. Kimi takes no interactive task, so it gets it by `hc send` once its own input line shows, after its folder trust for this work tree is answered once, as in Rex. When hc says the launch task was not sent (`first_message.sent` false), the script stops without resending it. - **How the script knows what the reviewer is doing.** A reported status (OSC 7501, read with `hc get`) comes first; Codex 0.166 reported one on 2026-10-29, and its turn count says when it has worked. A reviewer that reports none, as the Cursor agent v2026.10.22 did not, is read from the bottom of its screen with Rex's patterns: usage limit, question, trust dialog, busy marker, unsent prompt, its own empty input line. Blocked is a question for the owner: the script stops after two minutes of it and never types past it. - **Pacing.** Looks are paced by `hc wait --timeout`, which returns early when the reviewer's state changes; when it returns at once (a reviewer already idle), the script sleeps the interval. - **The exits are the same.** On exit 0 the script ends and removes the reviewer's terminal (`hc kill`, then `hc rm`), and only that one. On exit 1 it leaves the terminal running; `Next:` reads it with `hc read ` or waits with `hc wait `, and an answer goes in with `hc attach ` or `hc keys `. Never stop the hc server: every terminal on the machine runs in it. **Without Herdr, Rex or the Herdr app** (the working agent is in none of them), when the order reaches Codex, run it through the Codex plugin: ```sh node "$(ls -d "$HOME"/.claude/plugins/cache/openai-codex/codex/*/scripts/codex-companion.mjs | tail -1)" \ adversarial-review --wait --base main --scope branch --model gpt-6-luna "" ``` The plugin takes `--model` but no effort setting, so the review runs at the `model_reasoning_effort` in `~/.codex/config.toml`. Tell it which claims to verify and which documents must stay consistent. Ask it to be adversarial, and to say how the thing under review could still pass while being wrong. - **State claims as the change's effects, not as your search.** Name what the change does to the project, in this PR's own terms. For example, a PR that adds an order status and drops a manual approval step should claim "orders gain a status; refunds no longer wait for manual approval", not "every document stating the counts was updated". The reviewer checks what the claim names, so a claim that describes your search confines the review to the places you already looked. - **Reproduce every finding before you accept it.** A finding is a claim; run it. A finding accepted on assertion becomes a wrong change. - **Fix every place a finding applies, not only the one it names.** Before you fix a finding, name its kind, such as a wording, a rule, or a value crossing a boundary, and search the whole repository for it with the project's search tool. Fix every instance in the same commit, and tell the next round the kind and the search you ran. The review scripts ask the reviewer for the same list, but a reviewer can judge one instance fine and leave it out. One PR took three holds this way, each on a named reference crossing a different validation stage; another took a hold for a gate's scope fixed in two of the three documents that stated it. Name the class, not the instance: a finding about one spelling of a path is about every spelling, and one about one exit path of a script (a signal, a timeout, a hang at exit) is about every exit path. List the class in your reply and test each member, as "Prove a new check fails" below describes. On 2026-10-24 a guard took four further reviews, each finding a rarer spelling of a path, and a review script took six, each finding another exit path. - **Fix clear defects; answer judgement calls in the PR body.** Say which is which, so the reviewer can weigh the judgement. - **Re-review after fixing, at most two rounds.** A fix can introduce its own defects — a guard tightened in one place is often loosened in another — so run the review again on the fixed diff. A round is one independent review of the branch's head. The limit applies per batch of work: - Before the pull request opens, at most two rounds. - Each HOLD on the open pull request starts a fresh count of two for the fixes it asks for. After the second round of a batch, fix only a finding that would let a wrong result through on input the project will realistically see. This holds for a project's quick checks of later fixes too: a rarer member of a class the change already covers, such as one more encoding of a path, is a follow-up or a judgement call in the PR body, not another fix. List every other finding in the PR body as a follow-up. Push the last fix without another review, and name that unreviewed commit in the PR body. If round two finds the same kind of defect as round one, redesign (next point) instead of patching a third time. - **Redesign when tightening a rule starts flagging a *correct* case.** That is the stop signal: a rule tightened to catch one variant of a defect now fails on a case which is right, and no further tightening converges from there — each attempt buys another review round. Change the design instead: what the rule reads, or where in the flow it sits. Say in the PR what design changed and why, then re-check the old variants under the new shape. Narrowing what a check claims is a redesign too: a check that scans text for every way to do a thing loses to the next spelling, while one that pins the exact output of the code that matters (the queries the counts, the hash and the round trip send, captured from a fake session) cannot. Say the narrower claim in the docs that describe the check. Until that redesign lands, variants of one wrong design are not separate bugs to be filed away — three copies of a stale figure are three real defects, and they stay defects. A redesign forced by round two gets one review of its own. That is the only review past the limit. ## Prove a new check fails When you add a check, break the thing it checks on purpose (change one figure, one status, one record) and confirm the check fails; then restore it. A check that has never failed may pass vacuously. Clear the interpreter's bytecode cache (`__pycache__` for Python) before each run of a mutation and after restoring it. A mutation the same length as the line it replaces, restored within the same second, can leave a cached copy of the mutant that the next run executes, so a correct tree fails or a broken one passes. Test the check against the cases it claims, not just the happy path: a guard that hashes names rather than contents, or that follows a symlink, or that reads a file named `-` as standard input, passes every ordinary run and fails none. Enumerate the cases the check claims to catch and make each one fail on purpose. When the cases form a class of input, such as any character or any spelling a renderer accepts, state the rule on what the renderer produces, not on the source text. Then generate the class in the test: every candidate character at every position. A list of the spellings you thought of is what a reviewer extends one round at a time. One check that a quoted answer renders as plain text took nine review rounds this way, most rounds finding another way to hide markup (indentation, a nested quote, zero-width and control characters). It converged only once the rule read the parser's output. The review that passed it tried every code point at nine positions, a probe the test should have run from the start. Confirm the test run finished before you read its result, from the runner's own final lines (for example `Ran 95 tests` and `FAILED (failures=20)`), not from a count of its output. A run that never starts or never finishes prints no final result, and a count piped from it still prints a number. One test meant to fail on the unfixed code read as zero failures because the command wrapping it was not installed, so `grep -c` counted the shell's error message. Run without the wrapper, it reported twenty failures. A test that **reproduces a defect** is held to the same standard: run it against the unfixed code and confirm it fails, for the reason you expect. That is not a rule for every new test. A compatibility or invariant test — a valid input still works, the same answer survives reformatting — passes both versions, and forcing it to fail would delete exactly the coverage `guardrails.md` asks for. But that holds only while the invariant already holds on the unfixed code. When the defect *is* that it does not — reformatting changes the answer — the test must fail there, and it is a defect test like any other. Watch too for a test that passes for the wrong reason: the input that looks like the bug is not always the one that exercises it. Take a check that reads backticked spans in documents and treats a digest-shaped one as a pin to verify. It must leave `docker compose up …` alone, where `…` means "and so on", so a test asserts exactly that — and it passed, on a span written the way the docs show it, `! docker compose up …`. The check removes the whitespace inside a span before asking whether the span is a pin at all, and the shell's `!` is no digit or letter, so that span failed on its first character and was never judged. The `!` was doing the work; the ellipsis was never tested. Drop the `!` and the same words join into `dockercomposeup…`, which passes for a digest, and the build fails on a documentation line — the case the test existed to cover. Same words, one character apart, and the assertion held in both runs for reasons that had nothing to do with each other. So state the input and the assertion, then say why the assertion held. If the reason is not the one you meant to test, the input is wrong. A test that checks data against a document (a fixture against its specification, a generated file against the table it encodes) compares every fact the document states, not just the identifiers. Comparing names and connections lets a wrong type, value or reference through. Two more steps close the gap: - **Forbid facts the document does not state.** Compare whole records for exact equality, so an invented value fails. - **Pin the document text the data was last checked against,** by hash, so any edit to that text fails the test until someone checks the data again. A parser reads only the facts it was written for and cannot notice an edit to the rest; the pin can. ## Done when All six hold, and the PR body says that they ran and what the review found. # Documents Read this when writing or restructuring a project's documents. ## One place per meaning - Each rule, status or figure has one authoritative place; other documents point to it. Two wordings drift apart, and the drift becomes a review round. - Instruction files (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`) load into every turn, so they hold pointers and the few rules an agent needs before acting. Move detail into docs and checks, and shrink the instruction file once a check enforces a rule. ## Method and record are separate - A **method** (playbook, standard) says how to do the work, company-neutral, and changes only when the method improves. - A **record** (worklog, decision records, backlog) says what happened on this project. - Project decisions go in the record; the method may cite them as worked examples. ## Moving approved text When approved text moves between files, move it word for word with a note naming its origin. Rewording approved text needs the owner's recorded decision. ## Dates A record dates an event by the day it happened in the time zone the project's conventions name, and says so once where the project keeps them. A project with no recorded convention records one before its first dated note, by default the owner's own time zone. A run that crosses midnight in UTC otherwise gets two dates for one landing, and a reviewer holds the record for the mismatch. ## Handover notes A handover brief outside the repo goes stale the moment work starts. When it is used, add a note at its top saying when, by which session, and where the outputs live; the repo is ground truth. ## Done when Every rule you touched has one authoritative wording, every other mention points to it, and the instruction file holds pointers rather than detail.

# Enterprise Context Engineering

> A reference architecture and build workspace for creating an evidence-grounded enterprise context layer that lets people and AI agents answer: **what happened, what changed, why a decision was made, what evidence supports that explanation, and what remains uncertain.**

## Why this repository exists

Enterprise knowledge is rarely held in one governed system. It is distributed across structured operational data, reports, dashboards, data models, spreadsheets, business-process artifacts, presentations, PDFs, emails, meeting notes, policies, work orders, and analytics outputs. The material may be correct in isolation but difficult to assemble into a trustworthy answer about the enterprise.

The problem is not merely document search. It is **context engineering**:

- connecting business concepts, processes, assets, data products, metrics, decisions, evidence, and outcomes;
- preserving the time and version in which an assertion was valid;
- distinguishing direct evidence from analytical inference and unknowns;
- retaining claim-level provenance to the source artifact, record, slide, page, query, or calculation that supports an answer; and
- giving human users and AI agents a governed way to retrieve, reason over, and explain enterprise context.

This repository develops that architecture using a realistic commercial/industrial example, including business intelligence, operations, planning, reliability, finance, and OT-adjacent information. It also provides a synthetic enterprise corpus so the approach can be built and evaluated without relying on confidential production data.

## Core questions

The intended system should support questions such as:

- What does this KPI mean, how is it calculated, what sources feed it, and who owns it?
- Which business process, capability, value-stream stage, asset, customer, or product does this metric describe?
- What changed between two reporting periods, source-system versions, or organizational configurations?
- Why was a historical operational, commercial, reliability, or planning decision made?
- Which facts are directly supported by records, which are inferred, and what cannot be determined from the available evidence?
- Which documents, emails, slides, work orders, historian windows, reports, and policies support the answer?
- How does a source-system field travel through ingestion, transformation, semantic modeling, KPI calculation, and a consuming report or agent answer?

## Architectural thesis

The platform is a **context layer**, not a replacement for operational systems, a conventional document repository, or a generic vector database. It combines five complementary layers:

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Source and evidence layer | Preserves structured records, documents, presentations, messages, reports, and OT/operational observations with source metadata |
| Semantic layer | Defines shared business vocabulary, ontology, taxonomy, domain models, data contracts, and mappings |
| Provenance and decision layer | Connects claims, evidence, decisions, alternatives, constraints, actors/roles, outcomes, and time validity |
| Retrieval and reasoning layer | Retrieves relevant evidence and graph context; composes bounded, cited answers; exposes uncertainty and contradiction |
| Governance and evaluation layer | Applies access control, source classification, quality validation, lineage, release control, and repeatable evaluation |

The guiding principle is:

> An answer is trustworthy only when its claims can be traced to evidence, its assumptions and inferences are visible, its temporal context is respected, and unknowns remain unknown.

## Position relative to EPM and PPC

This repository remains a **context-layer and evaluation framework**. It is not a downstream enterprise simulation, a performance-management application, or an autonomous-agent platform. Its relationship to EPM and PPC is deliberate:

- **EPM (Enterprise Performance Model)** defines what the downstream enterprise means and how performance is represented, including the Downstream Oil and Gas Ontology (the same artifact earlier referred to as the "LSC ontology"). **Proposed:** ECE imports that ontology rather than forking it; this is still an open decision in the [project charter](docs/charter.md) (section 7, item 3).
- **ECE (this repository)** defines how trustworthy enterprise context is assembled, grounded, temporally bounded, traced to evidence, and evaluated.
- **PPC (Pearland Petroleum Corporation)** is a downstream proving ground that integrates both. **Proposed:** it consumes versioned ECE contracts once they are published; it is not an ECE runtime dependency, and ECE does not need PPC to build or validate its own artifacts.

**Lagos Specialty Chemicals (LSC)** is ECE's own worked-example scenario for the synthetic corpus and the knowledge-source inventory. It is a separate fictitious enterprise from PPC, which is a different downstream company.

The relationships above are proposed, matching the `Status: Proposed` of the two architecture documents linked below.

> EPM defines enterprise meaning. ECE defines trustworthy context. PPC proves that both can operate together.

Technology is reused across these efforts, but project truth is not: **share platform patterns and reusable code; keep project truth, semantics, releases, and access boundaries separate.** See the [Shared Technical Foundation](docs/architecture/shared-technical-foundation.md) and the [EPM–ECE–PPC Operating Model](docs/architecture/epm-ece-ppc-operating-model.md).

## Synthetic decision provenance

A central capability of this repository is a **synthetic decision-provenance corpus**. Traditional synthetic data often covers transactions, master data, telemetry, alarms, work orders, or reports. It usually lacks the reasoning context that explains why people selected one option over another.

This project fills that gap by creating a fictional but internally consistent enterprise history in which decisions are distributed across realistic artifacts:

- email threads and approval exchanges;
- meeting minutes and action logs;
- PowerPoint review decks and option analyses;
- decision memoranda, policies, and procedures;
- planning, finance, reliability, maintenance, and operational reports;
- CMMS/work-order, ERP, laboratory, historian, and alarm summaries; and
- later outcome reports, exceptions, and retrospective reviews.

The corpus is explicitly **synthetic**. It is not a reconstruction of real historical decisions and must never be represented as factual organizational history. Its purpose is to train, demonstrate, and evaluate the system’s ability to recover a decision rationale from fragmented evidence without inventing unsupported facts.

The canonical synthetic decision ledger is the hidden truth layer. Generated artifacts intentionally reveal only portions of that truth. The agent is evaluated on whether it can assemble a grounded explanation from the evidence available to it.

See [the synthetic data generation strategy](docs/strategy/synthetic-data-generation-strategy.md).

## Design principles

- **Evidence before fluency.** Retrieval and source attribution take precedence over a polished narrative.
- **Claim-level provenance.** Material claims point to a source artifact and precise location where practical.
- **Time-aware context.** Distinguish authoring time, decision time, effective period, ingestion time, and superseded versus current versions.
- **Evidence, inference, unknown.** Responses must label what is observed, inferred, contradictory, and unavailable.
- **Semantic interoperability.** Use explicit domain vocabulary and mappings rather than embedding critical meaning only in prompts or prose.
- **Synthetic by design.** All generated records and documents carry synthetic provenance, scenario, seed, generator, and release metadata.
- **Separate truth from retrieval.** Hidden generation truth is used for validation and evaluation, never supplied to the answering agent in a test.
- **Reproducibility.** Scenarios, schemas, generator versions, seeds, manifests, checksums, and validation results are versioned.
- **Governance by construction.** Access, retention, source classification, and evaluation isolation are architecture requirements—not cleanup tasks.
- **Two axes, not one.** Track *source/data classification* (what an artifact is and how it may be handled: synthetic, development, validation, hidden; source-system profile) separately from *epistemic status* (what a statement is: direct evidence, inference, contradiction, unknown). Neither implies the other.
- **Share patterns, not project truth.** Reuse technology, helper code, and deployment patterns freely; never share one project's data bucket, hidden truth, release namespace, or domain configuration.

## Proposed repository structure

The repository is evolving toward the following structure. Existing discovery and architecture materials can be retained during migration, then linked or reorganized into these durable areas. Paths below are targets, not current locations — some directories (e.g. `docs/examples/`, `docs/governance/`) do not exist yet.

Large generated data, document bundles, rendered artifacts, Parquet data, graph exports, and hidden evaluation truth should not be committed to Git. Store them in controlled object storage with versioned manifests. See the Cloudflare R2 workflow in [docs/strategy/cloudflare-r2-data-storage-and-agent-workflow.md](docs/strategy/cloudflare-r2-data-storage-and-agent-workflow.md).

## Build flow

1. **Define the semantic and scenario model** — enterprise domains, business capabilities, processes, assets, products, organizations, roles, decisions, evidence, constraints, outcomes, and temporal rules.
2. **Create canonical synthetic truth** — deterministic reference data, events, decision ledger, and expected outcomes.
3. **Generate evidence artifacts** — structured records, emails, reports, slides, memos, work orders, telemetry/event summaries, and outcome documents.
4. **Validate coherence** — schema conformance, referential integrity, temporal validity, engineering/business constraints, provenance, and controlled ambiguity.
5. **Build retrieval products** — document index, semantic graph, metadata/catalog entries, vector representations, and source-to-answer evidence links.
6. **Generate and run evaluations** — questions, expected evidence sets, gold answers, preference pairs, and hidden truth scoring.
7. **Publish a release** — manifest, checksums, release notes, validation results, and controlled exports.

## Current materials

The repository currently contains:

- end-to-end solution-architecture assets;
- discovery workbooks and build-roadmap material;
- analytical agent outputs and charts;
- a source-document example; and
- early architecture/rendering assets.

The proposed structure above provides the target organization for these materials as implementation moves from discovery toward repeatable semantic modeling, synthetic-data generation, retrieval, and evaluation.

## Getting started

1. Read the architecture and discovery materials already in the repository.
2. Read the [synthetic data generation strategy](docs/strategy/synthetic-data-generation-strategy.md).
3. Review the architecture and discovery materials; the ontology/domain model and competency questions are established in Phase 0 (see the [project charter](docs/charter.md)).
4. Start with a small scenario: one business unit, a limited asset/process scope, 10–20 decisions, and 4–6 artifact types per decision.
5. Build the hidden canonical ledger first, then generate distributed evidence artifacts from it.
6. Validate a question-answering agent against the hidden truth before scaling volume or scenario breadth.

## Status and scope

This is an architecture, discovery, and implementation workspace. It is not a production system, a source of real corporate history, legal advice, safety guidance, or an operational decision authority. All synthetic content must remain clearly labeled and governed as synthetic.
